title: Driving, Serious & Dangerous Faults
whatItIs: Examiners judge each fault against a defined outcome of safe driving and record it as a driving, serious or dangerous fault, or not at all.
keyFacts: To pass: no more than 15 driving faults and no serious or dangerous faults.
One driving fault does not fail the test, but a fault repeated throughout can be marked as serious.
Serious fault: potentially dangerous, or a breach of the law (e.g. ignoring a red light or a stop sign).
Dangerous fault: actual danger to the examiner, candidate, public or property, marked even if the examiner acts.
One or both 'show me, tell me' questions answered wrongly = one driving fault.
Fuel-efficient driving is assessed and debriefed but does not count towards the result.

items.title: Driving fault: low risk
items.text: Not a fail alone, e.g. another car must slow.

items.title: Serious fault: high risk
items.text: Fail, e.g. emerging without proper observation.

items.title: Dangerous fault: actual danger
items.text: Fail, e.g. examiner acts to avoid a collision.

a.label: Examiner gives advice
points: A fault is seen but there is no immediate danger

b.label: Examiner takes action (ETA)
points: Immediate intervention needed to stop it becoming dangerous
Verbal, or physical (dual controls or steering)

onTheTest.question: Your pupil's test ends with 14 driving faults and 1 serious fault. What is the result?
options: Pass, because there are fewer than 16 driving faults
Fail, because of the serious fault
Pass, if the serious fault was during a manoeuvre
Fail, because 14 driving faults is over the limit
onTheTest.why: To pass you need no more than 15 driving faults and no serious or dangerous faults. One serious fault is an immediate fail.

onTheTest.question: Which DT1 principle asks: 'If the drive was perfect before and after this fault, would this fault alone cause a fail?'
onTheTest.why: The first rule of assessment (DT1 11.06) makes the examiner judge each fault in isolation, on its own effect on safety, the law or control.

traps: The '16th fault' rule is about whether to record a fault at all: could you justify failing on it if it were the 16th?
A fault is never double-marked, but marking both control and observation on a manoeuvre is not double marking.
Experienced drivers on an extended test should not be penalised for driving to a higher standard than learners.
